teaser.text: Aviva is a financial-services company that sells protection against financial shocks, helps people build savings, and turns savings into retirement income. A pound enters mainly as an insurance premium, an investment fee or a loan repayment, and leaves through claims, customer benefits, operating costs and investment.

stock.title: Aviva stock forecast
stock.meta_description: Aviva's forecast weighs earnings growth, underwriting, Direct Line savings, capital generation and cash returns across bear, base and bull scenarios.
stock.opening: Aviva's weighted scenario points to 304.02p by October 2027 and 328.72p by October 2029; the bear case has 30% probability, the base case 55%, and the bull case 15%. It hinges on earnings growth, underwriting and Direct Line savings.
stock.closing: The full memo also explains Aviva's business, its rivals, its management and its risks.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for Aviva, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: Bear earnings fall to £734m and then £677m before recovering to £728m. Its margins are 2.7%, 2.4% and 2.5%, allowing for claims inflation, weak motor pricing and integration drag. Bull earnings reach £1,034m and £1,128m before £1,193m, on margins of 3.8%, 4.0% and 4.1%. That requires favourable claims, Wealth fees and Direct Line savings. All cases use revenue of £27.2bn, £28.2bn and £29.1bn, excluding the £195m disposal gain and £62m governance credit.

blocks.heading: How much does Aviva really earn and give back?

paragraphs.text: Operating own funds generation rose to £2,317 million in 2025. It measures capital created under Aviva’s Solvency II reporting, not necessarily money available for dividends. Cash remittances are different: they are payments from subsidiaries to the parent through dividends or internal-loan interest. They reached £2,077 million in 2025, while the £1.35 billion received for the Direct Line acquisition was excluded because acquisition funding is not recurring cash.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Aviva today?

paragraphs.text: The P/E, or price-to-earnings ratio, says how much investors pay for one pound of annual profit. Reported earnings include investment movements, changes in the value of insurance promises and acquisition charges. Operating earnings remove or smooth some of these effects. For the six months to June 2026, Aviva reported £1,326 million of operating profit and £418 million of IFRS profit. Operating EPS was 31.8p, while basic EPS was 12.2p. Market-data “core earnings” may use different adjustments, so neither measure should be accepted without checking its definition.

blocks.heading: What does Aviva pay shareholders per share?

paragraphs.text: Insurance revenue reached £25,437 million in 2025. The combined ratio improved to 94.6% in 2025. Operating return on equity rose from 9.4% in 2022 to 17.5% in 2025. EPS was 26.50p against a 35.74p dividend in 2025. Average diluted shares rose 6.5% in 2025 while buybacks were zero. The valuation is 41.4x trailing P/E and 2.4x price-to-book. The key cash-return figures are a 5.5% dividend yield and a 0.0% buyback yield.

Base dividends rise from 42p to 46p and then 50p. The declared 14p interim dividend and recent 39.3p annual payout support continued growth, while guidance calls for mid-single-digit cash-cost growth. The bear case gives 40p, then 38p and 38p, reflecting payout cover risk. The bull case gives 44p, 50p and 56p, requiring stronger earnings and remittances. Dividends already exceeded common earnings in 2025, so faster growth is not assumed automatically.

blocks.heading: Does Aviva's cash cover its dividend?

paragraphs.text: Aviva’s earnings for common shareholders were £767 million in the latest year, while ordinary dividends were £1,034 million. It made no ordinary share buybacks. The previous year’s distributions exceeded common earnings by £588 million.

Operating own funds generation rose to £2,317 million in 2025. It measures capital created under Aviva’s Solvency II reporting, not necessarily money available for dividends. Cash remittances are different: they are payments from subsidiaries to the parent through dividends or internal-loan interest. They reached £2,077 million in 2025, while the £1.35 billion received for the Direct Line acquisition was excluded because acquisition funding is not recurring cash.
